# Plugin Convention

A plugin is the seam between the environment and the application. Everything env-conditional lives here, and nothing else does.

## Scope

Applies to `*.plugin.ts` files and the file that registers them.

Does **not** apply to SDK clients ([sdk-client-convention.md](../node-backend/sdk-client-convention.md)), which receive resolved config and know nothing about where it came from.

## File and export naming

`{name}.plugin.ts` exporting `{name}Plugin`, kebab-case file, camelCase export. Never `register{Name}` — the suffix already says what it is.

## A plugin is a thin wrapper

It reads validated config, constructs one thing, decorates it, and stops.

```ts
// CORRECT — resolve config here, hand the client a finished object
export const s3Plugin = fp(async (fastify) => {
  const { AWS_REGION, S3_BUCKET, S3_ENDPOINT } = fastify.config;

  const storage = new S3Client(
    { s3ClientConfig: { region: AWS_REGION, endpoint: S3_ENDPOINT }, bucket: S3_BUCKET },
    fastify.log,
  );

  fastify.decorate('storage', storage);
});
```

Everything environment-shaped belongs here and nowhere deeper: falling back from one variable to another, omitting credentials so the SDK picks up an instance role, deriving `secure = port === 465`, choosing a provider by `NODE_ENV`. A client receives resolved config, never variable names — which means a plugin is the only place that reads `fastify.config`.

What stays **out** of a plugin:

- Business logic. If a plugin branches on domain state, that branch belongs in a service.
- HTTP error mapping. A client throws its own `{Vendor}{Condition}Error`; the consuming service maps it to an `AppError` subclass. A plugin that catches and rethrows as HTTP has put transport knowledge one layer too deep.
- Anything a second plugin also does. Two plugins constructing the same client is two sources of configuration.

A plugin that wraps a third-party Fastify plugin which already decorates the instance calls no `decorate` of its own — registering it is the whole job.

## Registration order is a declaration

Register every plugin in one file, in an explicit order, and treat that file as the source of truth. Where the order is load-bearing, say so in a comment next to the registration rather than in a document that will drift from it.

Order is load-bearing more often than it looks: config validation first, then connections, then anything that needs a connection at startup, then the registries that construct application objects from those connections.

## Registry plugins

Repositories and services are constructed **once**, in a registry plugin, and decorated onto the instance. Consumers resolve them from `fastify.xRepository` / `fastify.xService` — never construct one per route.

```
repository-registry.plugin.ts   constructs every repository from the decorated clients
service-registry.plugin.ts      constructs every service; registered last
```

The repository registry runs after the clients it needs and before the service registry; the service registry stays last, because a service may depend on anything. Adding a repository or service means editing its registry and the instance's type declaration — those two edits are the whole wiring, and keeping them together is why it is one file rather than a decorator scattered across the codebase.

## Lifecycle

A plugin that constructs a client owning a connection drives its lifecycle: `connect()` at registration, `close()` from an `onClose` hook. The client never calls either itself ([sdk-client-convention.md § Lifecycle](../node-backend/sdk-client-convention.md#lifecycle)).

## NEVER Do

- Name a plugin export `register{Name}`.
- Read `fastify.config` anywhere but a plugin.
- Put business logic or HTTP error mapping in a plugin.
- Construct the same client in two plugins.
- Construct a repository or service outside its registry plugin.
- Register the service registry before anything it might depend on.
- Let a client open its own connection at construction, or close it from inside.
